commits.pr_title: [ROCm][CI] Drop LD_PRELOAD from the subprocess env in test_amd_ci_fast_exit
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose
`:amd: (MI250) Docker Build Metadata` has been failing since today's nightly (Oct 30), after [#61939](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61939) added the `amd_ci_fast_exit` pytest plugin and its tests. Failing run: [ci#98597](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/98597/list?jid=01a18b6a-f5da-4f82-b9be-fe27164bdb2f&tab=output) (2 of 2 attempts). Four tests in `tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py` fail because the pytest subprocess they start ends with SIGSEGV:
```text
FAILED tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py::test_a_passing_run_exits_zero_despite_the_teardown_crash - AssertionError: Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
FAILED tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py::test_a_failing_run_keeps_its_exit_status - assert -11 == <ExitCode.TESTS_FAILED: 1>
FAILED tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py::test_python_exit_handlers_still_run - assert -11 == 0
FAILED tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py::test_a_nested_in_process_session_does_not_end_the_outer_one - AssertionError: Running 2 items in this shard
```

The plugin lets pytest exit before native teardown, so a crash there cannot fail a run whose tests passed. It turns itself off when a kernel recorder is loaded, and one of its checks is `rocprofiler` in `LD_PRELOAD`. The tests run pytest in a subprocess through `_run`, which removes the recorder variables `ROCP_TOOL_LIBRARIES` and `CUDA_INJECTION64_PATH` from the subprocess environment, but not `LD_PRELOAD`.

The nightly runs with the kernel recorder enabled, which puts `librocprofiler-sdk.so` in `LD_PRELOAD`. The subprocess inherits it, so the plugin turns itself off, and the teardown crash the tests simulate ends the process with SIGSEGV (`-11`). Builds without the recorder do not set it, so the tests pass there.

This PR removes `LD_PRELOAD` from the subprocess environment in `_run`, like the other recorder variables, and adds an `LD_PRELOAD` case to `test_off_when_disabled_or_a_kernel_recorder_needs_native_teardown`, so all three recorder checks are covered. Test-only change; the plugin is unchanged.

## Test Plan
MI300X (gfx942), in the `rocm/vllm-dev:ci_base` image, with the ROCProfiler SDK preloaded as in the nightly:
```bash
cd tests
LD_PRELOAD=/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/_rocm_sdk_devel/lib/librocprofiler-sdk.so \
  pytest -v -s tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py
```

## Test Result
Before:
```text
FAILED tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py::test_a_passing_run_exits_zero_despite_the_teardown_crash
FAILED tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py::test_a_failing_run_keeps_its_exit_status
FAILED tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py::test_python_exit_handlers_still_run
FAILED tools/test_amd_ci_fast_exit.py::test_a_nested_in_process_session_does_not_end_the_outer_one
4 failed, 4 passed
```
After:
```text
9 passed
```
This PR adds one test case (the `LD_PRELOAD` case), so it runs 9 tests instead of 8.

AI-assisted tooling was used to analyze the CI logs and to run the validation. The results and the change were manually reviewed.

commits.pr_title: [Multimodal] Cache PyNvVideoCodec decoder caps
commits.pr_body:
## Overview The PyNvVideoCodec (NVDEC) video backend calls `nvc.GetDecoderCaps` on every request, from `PyNvVideoCodecVideoBackendMixin._validate_decoder_caps`. Each call takes ~180 ms and holds the GIL, so it freezes the whole API server process for that long. The result only depends on the device, codec, chroma format and bit depth, so this PR caches it in a bounded LRU (64 entries). ## Claims - **Removes ~185 ms of fixed cost from every NVDEC video request.** The caps check drops from 183–190 ms to 0.3–1.6 ms. It also removes the ~180 ms freeze of the API server's event loop per request. - **Serving:** Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni NVFP4 on 1× GB300 with the default config: TTFT −19 to −45% and throughput 1.37–1.90× for clips up to ~30 s. Longer videos see −2 to −7% TTFT, because decoding dominates. - **No regressions:** - Decoded frames are byte-identical, and unsupported videos are still rejected. - In the worst case, every lookup misses, and loading performs the same as main: latency within ±1%, throughput 1.00–1.02×. - **Bounded:** at most 64 entries per API server process, 27 KiB when full. Real deployments use a handful. ## Validation ### Media loading, no model, 1× GB300 **Setup:** - **Script:** `bench_pynvvideocodec_caps.py`, attached to this PR. It is not part of the change. - **Code path:** the API server's own path for local videos, `MediaConnector.fetch_video_async("file://…")`, decoding on the server's media thread pool. - **Video kwargs:** `{"backend": "pynvvideocodec", "num_frames": 256, "fps": 2, "hw_decoders": 2, "max_width": 1920, "max_height": 1920}`. - **Runs:** 3 repetitions. Each arm runs in a fresh process, and the arm order alternates between repetitions. - **Videos:** 12 real videos per row. - **Arms:** - "main" is `GetDecoderCaps` on every request. That matches main's own module; see below. - "PR" is this change. - "Worst case" clears the cache before every lookup, so every lookup misses. | Videos (sampled frames) | Latency, 1 in flight, ms: main → PR | Δ [95% CI] | req/s at 8 in flight: main → PR | Event loop stalled at 8 in flight: main → PR | Worst case vs main: latency, req/s | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 5 s, 480×320, H.264 (10) | 199 → 15 | **−92%** [−95, −90] | 5.3 → 107 (**20×**) | 98% → 0% | −0%, 1.00× | | 4 s, 392×240, VP9 (8) | 194 → 10 | **−95%** [−96, −95] | 5.3 → 177 (**34×**) | 98% → 0% | −0%, 1.00× | | 13 s, 1080p, H.264 (24) | 363 → 175 | **−52%** [−55, −49] | 4.5 → 10.5 (**2.3×**) | 93% → 0% | −0%, 1.00× | | 20 s, 1024×520, MPEG-4 Part 2 (39), 10 of 12 decodable | 574 → 388 | **−32%** [−53, −22] | 3.0 → 3.9 (1.3×) | 60% → 0% | +0%, 1.02× | | 31 s, 720p, H.264 (61) | 380 → 190 | **−50%** [−54, −46] | 4.2 → 9.8 (**2.3×**) | 85% → 0% | −0%, 1.00× | | 9 min, 720p, H.264 (256) | 2,641 → 2,453 | −7% [−8, −6] | 0.72 → 0.76 (1.06×) | 17% → 2% | +0%, 1.00× | How to read the table: - **Latency** is paired by video. Each interval is a 95% bootstrap over videos. - **"Event loop stalled"** is the share of wall time the server's asyncio loop woke more than 10 ms late. Without the cache, back-to-back `GetDecoderCaps` calls froze it for up to 1.3 s at a time. - **Decoded frames** (SHA-256 of all frames plus the sampled indices) are identical across all arms and repetitions for all 72 videos. The 2 MPEG-4 videos NVDEC can't decode are rejected in every run. **"main" is main.** The same arm run against main's own `pynvvideocodec.py` (3 more repetitions) matches the PR build's `uncached` arm within 0.3% latency (all 95% CIs within ±0.7%). Throughput, caps-check time and event-loop stall are the same, and decoded frames are byte-identical.
Full benchmark output and how to reproduce ```bash python bench_pynvvideocodec_caps.py
### Serving **Setup:** - **Commit:** #57924's merge commit (5a4f307d). `pynvvideocodec.py` is unchanged from there to this PR's base. - **Model:** Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B-A3B-Reasoning NVFP4 on 1× GB300. - **Server:** - 1 API server with `hw_decoders=2`. - 2 fps, at most 256 frames, `--video-pruning-rate 0.5`. - CUDA MPS on. Prefix cache and multimodal processor cache off. - **Workload:** 12 real videos per row (Video-MME, MVBench, NExT-QA, MSR-VTT, VDC), sent by `file://`. 128 output tokens, `ignore_eos`. - **Metrics:** - TTFT is with one request in flight, paired by video, with a 95% bootstrap interval. - Throughput is at 8 in flight, over 48 requests. - One repetition. | Video (sampled frames) | TTFT, one in flight, ms: main → PR | Δ [95% CI] | req/s at 8 in flight | Server CPU s/req | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 5 s, ≤360p (10) | 517 → 283 | **−45%** [−64, −28] | 3.56 → 6.75 (**1.90×**) | 0.3 → 0.2 | | 13 s, 1080p (25) | 670 → 520 | **−22%** [−24, −21] | 2.83 → 4.65 (**1.64×**) | 0.8 → 0.5 | | 30 s, 720p (61) | 802 → 650 | **−19%** [−21, −17] | 2.26 → 3.26 (**1.44×**) | 0.9 → 0.8 | | 1.5 min, 720p (175) | 2,062 → 1,909 | −7% [−9, −6] | 1.09 → 1.17 (1.08×) | 1.9 → 1.7 | | 7 min, 360p (256) | 2,294 → 2,227 | −3% [−8, +5] | 0.98 → 1.09 (1.11×) | 2.6 → 2.4 | | 9 min, 720p (256) | 4,283 → 4,127 | −4% [−4, −3] | 0.63 → 0.65 (1.04×) | 3.5 → 3.3 | | 40 min, 720p (256) | 6,256 → 6,106 | −2% [−3, −2] | 0.39 → 0.39 (1.02×) | 4.4 → 4.1 | | 20 s MPEG-4 Part 2 (40), 9 of 12 decodable | 805 → 638 | **−21%** [−29, −15] | 2.23 → 3.06 (**1.37×**) | 0.7 → 0.5 |
Tuned config (4 API servers × hw_decoders=2), with OpenCV ×4 for reference | Video | TTFT, one in flight, ms: main → PR | req/s at 8 in flight: main → PR | OpenCV ×4 req/s | Server CPU s/req, OpenCV ×4 vs PR | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 30 s, 720p | 904 → 728, −19% [−23, −17] | 2.45 → **4.44** (1.81×) | 3.94 | 3.6 vs 0.7 | | 9 min, 720p | 4,300 → 4,118, −4% [−5, −4] | 1.05 → 1.15 (1.10×) | 1.28 | 27.4 vs 3.2 | | 40 min, 720p | 6,274 → 6,103, −3% [−3, −3] | 0.75 → **0.82** (1.09×) | 0.44 | 107 vs 4.2 |
### Tests and checks All on this PR's base (4b47db922b), 1× GB300: ```bash pytest tests/multimodal/test_video.py tests/multimodal/media/test_video.py ``` All PyNvVideoCodec tests pass, including the new one: 136 passed, 2 skipped, 11 failed. The 11 failures are the torchcodec tests (`test_torchcodec_*`, `test_video_loader_frames_sampling[*torchcodec*]` and `test_glm5next_backend_codec_parity[torchcodec]`). They fail the same way on main on this host, which has no system FFmpeg for torchcodec to load. The new test fails without the cache. Here the call site is reverted to main's `nvc.GetDecoderCaps(...)`: ``` > assert calls == ["h264", "hevc"] E AssertionError: assert ['h264', 'h26...hevc', 'hevc'] == ['h264', 'hevc'] E At index 1 diff: 'h264' != 'hevc' E Left contains 2 more items, first extra item: 'hevc' 1 failed, 108 deselected ``` ```bash pre-commit run --all-files --hook-stage manual # as in CI ``` All hooks pass, including mypy. There is no model evaluation: the change doesn't alter model inputs. The benchmark checks that decoded frames are byte-identical. ## Details ### Why a bounded LRU - **Caps never change while the server runs.** `GetDecoderCaps` reports what the GPU and driver can decode for a given (device, codec, chroma format, bit depth). Nothing in a request changes that, so the cache needs no invalidation. vLLM only reads `supported`, the width and height limits and `mb_num_max` from the result. - **The cache must be bounded.** The key is read from the uploaded file's stream headers, so an unbounded cache (`functools.cache`) would grow with every new format a client sends. `functools.lru_cache(maxsize=64)` caps memory with one decorator and keeps the formats in use resident. - **Why not per decoder slot.** Caps depend on the device and stream format, not on a slot: - One slot serves every format the traffic contains. On GB300, a single slot decoded H.264 → VP9 → H.264 → MPEG-4 → VP9 through `reconfigure_decoder`, without a rebuild. - Caps are needed before a slot is borrowed: they reject unsupported streams and set the maximum dimensions the slot's decoder is configured with. - A per-slot copy would miss on every format switch and after every slot recovery, and a client can trigger slot recoveries by sending corrupt videos. ### Why 64 - **Far above real use.** A deployment sees a handful of keys per device, for example H.264, HEVC, VP9 and AV1 at 4:2:0, 8- or 10-bit. With 64 entries, steady-state traffic always hits. - **Deliberately below the full key space.** PyNvVideoCodec has 12 compressed codecs × 4 chroma formats × 8, 10 or 12 bits, about 144 combinations per device. Most of those match no real video. The bound only needs to stop unbounded growth, not hold every possible key. - **Overflow is no worse than main.** If traffic cycles through more than 64 formats, lookups miss and each request calls `GetDecoderCaps`, as main does today. The benchmark's "worst case" column misses on every lookup and matches main within ±1%. - **Cheap when full.** Each entry is a 10-key dict. A full cache measured 26.9 KiB with `tracemalloc`, 431 B per entry. - **Not a tuning knob.** Any size between the number of formats in use and a few hundred performs the same. 64 is a round number with an order of magnitude of headroom. ### Other details - **`nvc` is part of the key.** Production always passes the PyNvVideoCodec module, so this costs nothing. It stops the existing tests' fake `nvc` classes, which return different caps for the same codec, from sharing entries. - **Threads.** `lru_cache` is safe to call from the media thread pool. Two requests racing on a cold key may each call `GetDecoderCaps` once, which is harmless. - **Failures.** A `supported == 0` result is cached, and the existing checks still reject the video. If `GetDecoderCaps` raises, nothing is cached. - **Shared result.** Callers get the same dict object. `_validate_decoder_caps` only reads it, and the docstring says not to mutate it. - **CI.** The new test uses a fake `nvc`, like the neighboring decoder-caps tests, so it needs no GPU. The existing `pytest -m 'not cpu_test' multimodal` Buildkite step picks it up. - **Not a duplicate.** I searched open PRs for `GetDecoderCaps`, "pynvvideocodec caps" and "decoder caps" and found none. #52605 also edits these two files (pool lease accounting), but in different hunks, and it merges cleanly with this PR. - **Out of scope.** `GetDecoderCaps` itself is slow and doesn't release the GIL. That is worth raising with the PyNvVideoCodec maintainers separately. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to port and test this change and to write and run the benchmark script. ---

(Mandatory for agents, optional for humans). - [x] AI assistance was used during the creation of this PR. - [x] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity. - [x] **Testing and Validation:** Validates the change and ensures any added tests are meaningful and reliable, with CI coverage or documented CI resource constraints and validation performed outside CI. - [x] **Code Quality and Style:** Keeps code and comments clear and concise, and updates relevant documentation and examples. - [x] **Pull Request Contents:** Includes a brief summary and relevant links, supports claims with evidence, explains root causes and implementation trade-offs, and follows the contributing guide.

commits.pr_title: [Qwen4Exp] PLE disk offload
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Adds `--engram-config '{"disk_offload": true}'` for Qwen4Exp. The PLE n-gram table stays in the checkpoint files, and each step reads only its rows on the host. On DGX Spark (GB10), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next NVFP4 loads with 27.0 GiB less memory. Decode is within 3.5% of the resident table, and GSM8K is unchanged.

This carries forward @Trosfy's design from #58815 (their commits are kept, co-authored). It is rebased onto the NVFP4 PLE tables from #56273 and renamed `disk_offload` to pair with `cpu_offload`.

## Claims

- **Memory:** no table in GPU or pinned host memory, and no copy in an offload directory. Recently read rows sit in the OS page cache, which the kernel can reclaim. The page cache does fill up over a long session (ids are hashed, so there is no locality), but the kernel reclaims it on demand without hurting decode; the cost of a cold table is in TTFT (below). Use it with the checkpoint on local NVMe: on network storage a cold prefill is 2 to 4.5x slower. On unified-memory Spark, `cpu_offload` does not help, because pinned memory comes out of the same pool as the weights and the KV cache.
- **Formats:** BF16, FP8 and NVFP4. Rows are read in checkpoint format and decoded on the GPU with the existing PLE kernel.
- **CUDA graphs:** the forward reads fixed device buffers, so graphs replay unchanged.
- **Cost:** decode within 3.5% at c=1/4/8, and about 11% higher TTFT.

## Validation

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 (`local-inference-lab@6c01ac3`), one GB10, both arms in one job on the same node. MTP n=3, FP8 KV (6 GiB), prefix caching off.

| | Resident | `disk_offload` | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weights loaded | 99.09 GiB | 72.09 GiB | -27.0 GiB |
| Host `MemAvailable` after startup | 4.6 GiB | 32.0 GiB | +27.4 GiB |
| Decode tok/s/user, c=1 | 33.63 | 32.45 | -3.5% |
| Decode tok/s, c=4 | 72.57 | 73.33 | +1.0% |
| Decode tok/s, c=8 | 94.04 | 91.99 | -2.2% |
| MTP acceptance length, c=1 | 2.33 | 2.31 | flat |
| TTFT, 8K prompt (median of 15) | 2540 ms | 2820 ms | +11.0% |
| GSM8K | 247/256 | 246/256 | -1 |

- Decode: aiperf, SPEED-Bench coding prompts, 1024 output tokens, active decode time only. One run per arm, so noise is a few percent.
- TTFT: exact-length random token ids with `max_tokens=1`. With the page cache dropped, the first 8K request took 3018 ms.
- The image was `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly-5555a2d8f7`, with every file touched by this PR and #56273 overlaid from this branch.
- CI: the H200 and CPU Qwen4 Exp lanes run the new tests. The Spark numbers were measured outside CI because there is no GB10 lane. On GB10 the new tests pass for all three formats.

### Cold cache and memory pressure

Same PR head (`396e7e0102`) and serve command, checkpoint on the node's local NVMe (ext4), one GB10. Page-cache residency is measured with `mincore` over the PLE shards; the memory cap is a cgroup `memory.max` on the container (GPU allocations are not charged to it). Short runs (3 to 6 rounds), so decode differences under ~10% are within noise.

| | Table in page cache | Decode c=1 | TTFT, 8K prompt | Disk read per 8K prefill |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Resident table | n/a | 40.1 tok/s | 2597 ms | 0 |
| `disk_offload`, warm (prompt rows cached for TTFT) | 8 to 25% | 35.8 tok/s | 2832 ms | 0 |
| `disk_offload`, page cache dropped before every request | 0% | 36.3 tok/s | 3110 ms | 1.04 GB |
| `disk_offload`, cgroup cap leaving 2 GiB for page cache | held at 4.7% | 37.6 tok/s | 3174 ms | 1.0 GB |
| `disk_offload`, checkpoint on NFS, cold | 0% | 34.5 tok/s | 6547 ms | 1.04 GB |

- Decode reads 5 to 17 MB/s from disk in every state, so it does not depend on the cache; c=4 aggregate stays at 81 to 90 tok/s cold and capped.
- A cold 8K prefill reads about 1 GB (300 to 330 MB/s on NVMe): +20% TTFT vs the resident table. Each PLE row is 80 B of NVFP4 weights plus 10 B of scales in separate tensors, so a lookup touches two 4 KiB pages; bytes read from disk were 3.6x the bytes requested.
- Without memory pressure the cached part of the table grows linearly, about 0.36% of the table per 1K generated tokens (11.8% after 33K tokens, no plateau). When memory is needed, the kernel reclaims it with no decode loss (residency held at 4.7% under the 2 GiB cap).

<details>
<summary>Commands</summary>

```bash
vllm serve local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 --language-model-only \
  --max-model-len 32768 --max-num-seqs 8 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --kv-cache-memory-bytes 6G --gpu-memory-utilization 0.87 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --speculative-config '{"method": "mtp", "num_speculative_tokens": 3}' \
  --compilation-config '{"max_cudagraph_capture_size": 32}' \
  --engram-config '{"disk_offload": true}'   # resident: '{"cpu_offload": false}'

pytest tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_ple.py tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_config.py
pytest tests/test_config.py -k engram
```

</details>

## Details

- **Load:** the default loader hands over zero-copy safetensors mmap views. Their file and offset are found in `/proc/self/maps`, the files are opened read-only, and the views are released. Loading fails if the shards do not cover the table, if a dtype does not match, or if a view is not file-backed (for example `.bin` or `fastsafetensors`).
- **Per step:** `Qwen4ExpModelState.prepare_inputs` computes and deduplicates the n-gram ids, reads each row with `preadv` (after a `WILLNEED` read-ahead hint), and copies the rows to the staging buffers.
- **Parallelism:** every TP rank stages full rows, so no ETP reduction is needed. Elastic EP is rejected.
- **Alternatives:** #58439 reads the checkpoint mapping from the GPU through host page tables. #54070 writes a second copy of the table to disk. This PR reads rows on the host from the files the loader already opened.

This PR does not batch the per-row reads for long prefills (that is the TTFT cost), change the checkpoint layout (rows and scales in one tensor would halve the pages per lookup), or support weight reload.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][HiSparse] Reserve in-flight imports' host pages at admission
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fixes #62217. Alternative to #62230.

HiSparse admits an async KV load only if its prompt fits in free host pages, but it ignores pages that earlier admitted loads still need. Two waiting loads can each hold pages the other needs. Waiting requests are never preempted, so the scheduler stalls forever with `running == []`.

Fix: reserve host pages for admitted loads, as `reserved_blocks` does for the GPU pool. The change is confined to `HiSparseSourceManager` and `HiSparseCoordinator`; the scheduler loop is unchanged.

- At admission of a load, `HiSparseSourceManager` sizes its host pages (prompt + spec decode step) and admits it only if they fit beside the pages other loads still need.
- The coordinator keeps a running total of outstanding pages (O(1) check), reduced as each load allocates its pages and dropped when the request is freed.
- Local admissions are not gated (they can be preempted), matching the GPU pool.

Alternatives: #62230 skips past held waiting requests in the scheduler loop. It changes the core loop, can starve the head of the queue, and still deadlocks when no admitted load fits.

Trade-off: a load whose host pages don't fit beside those reserved for in-flight loads waits for them, instead of being admitted and risking the deadlock.

## Test Plan

```bash
# Repro: both cases fail on main ({'first', 'second'} == {'first'}), pass here
pytest tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py -k test_hisparse_admitted_async_loads_can_finish_with_nothing_running

pytest tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hisparse_connector.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_hisparse_stats.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_remote_prefill_lifecycle.py
pytest tests/v1/e2e/general/test_hisparse.py   # 1x H100
```

New/extended tests in `tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py`:
- `test_hisparse_admitted_async_loads_can_finish_with_nothing_running`: the issue's scenario, plus an MTP case where the first load to resume has no host page for its draft tokens.
- `test_hisparse_async_admission_fits_beside_inflight_import`: boundary case, a load that exactly fits is admitted.
- `test_hisparse_import_reservation_released`: released on free and on resume.
- `test_hisparse_import_reservation_does_not_gate_local_admissions`.

## Test Result

- Unit (CPU): all pass. 3 unrelated failures (`test_async_scheduling_pp_allows_rescheduling_with_output_placeholders`, `test_draft_layer_rows_mirrored_after_drafter[FULL|NONE]`) fail identically on `main` locally.
- E2E (1x H100, `f96ae2830d`): `test_hisparse.py` 5 passed (`standalone-fa4` skips on SM90). New path exercised: in the `offload` case (HiSparse + OffloadingConnector), a coordinator probe logged the load sized at 5 pages, a 2-page reservation, and its release to 0 on resume.

## Performance

GLM-5.3-NVFP4 P/D on 8x B200: TP4 NIXL prefiller + TP4 HiSparse decoder (`MultiConnector[HiSparse, Nixl]`, `host_pool_gib=8`), `--kv-cache-dtype fp8 --block-size 64 --no-enable-prefix-caching`, `--speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'` on both servers.

```bash
vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 16384 --random-output-len 512 \
  --num-prompts 128 --max-concurrency 32 --ignore-eos --seed 42
```

Fresh decoder per run, interleaved. NIXL over TCP (no IB on that node), so the run is transfer-bound with the host pool ~96% full.

| Decoder | Output tok/s (2 runs) | Mean TTFT | Mean TPOT |
|---|---|---|---|
| PR (`c02494d57c`) | 191.52, 184.44 | 68.9 s, 72.3 s | 17.00, 16.82 ms |
| `main` (`cc1a6d3135`) | 182.61, 185.10 | 73.2 s, 73.0 s | 17.26, 16.33 ms |

No regression; at most 11 of 2,949 host pages were reserved. Without MTP, a P/D load allocates all its host pages at admission and nothing is reserved, so admission matches `main` exactly (verified on an earlier revision over IB: 580–581 tok/s in both arms).

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][KV Offload] Preserve stored event prefix order
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Preserve offload store key order so self-describing `BlockStored` events remain
parent-before-child within a transfer job. This prevents KV-aware routers from
dropping child blocks when a parent mapping has not been indexed yet.

## Claims

- Keep `TransferJobStatus.keys` in prefix order and deduplicate keys while
  retaining their first occurrence.
- Do not change the KV-event wire format or guarantee ordering across separate
  secondary-tier jobs, tiers, or promotion events; router-side pending/replay
  still covers those cases.

## Validation

- `pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_events.py -q`:
  51 passed.
- `pytest tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_scheduler.py -q`
  with the affected cases selected: 100 passed.
- `pre-commit run --files <changed-files>`: passed.
- Model evaluation is not applicable because this changes event ordering only.

## Details

The missing prefix order resulted from three assumptions rather than a decision
that order was unnecessary:

- [`#39186`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/39186) introduced
  `TransferJobStatus.keys` as set-backed job bookkeeping before offload events
  existed.
- [`#43468`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43468) made stored events
  self-describing and explicitly treated key order as irrelevant because each
  payload contains its parent hash. The order-independent test and
  “key order is free” comment codified that assumption.
- A consumer test in
  [`#52103`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52103#issuecomment-6251409146)
  later showed that llm-d still needs the parent event indexed first. The author
  confirmed the gap in
  [this reply](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52103#issuecomment-6255856451).

`prepare_store()` returns keys in prefix order, but the scheduler stored them in
a set. This can emit a child first even when transfer completion is FIFO. The
scheduler now preserves job order without removing set-style deduplication.

Secondary tiers are intentionally outside the ordering guarantee. FS/OBJ jobs
complete asynchronously and may become distinct raw events; tier aggregation
emits primary and secondary events by tier, not by parent topology. Therefore
this change fixes intra-job ordering but does not reorder across secondary jobs,
tiers, or promotions. Those cases remain a consumer concern.

Duplicate-work check: no open PR directly fixes this ordering path. #63129
addresses reused-key metadata lifecycle, and #52103 refactors event provenance
and removals while still retaining set-backed job keys.

AI assistance was used for investigation, implementation, and tests. The human
submitter must review every changed line and rerun the validation above.

commits.pr_title: [hw-agnostic] Opt-in infrastructure for OOT plugins
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Makes the Transformers backend's private `_resolve` public as `vllm.model_executor.hw_agnostic.resolve`, so out-of-tree plugins can register overrides that reach the layer class vLLM builds. The environment variable `VLLM_USE_HW_AGNOSTIC` is still orthogonal and can be used to choose whether the in-tree or the hw-agnostic implementations should be used. The Transformers backend resolves its layers through the same function.

Usage example:

  ```python
  RMSNorm = hw_agnostic.resolve("layernorm", "RMSNorm")

  @RMSNorm.register_oot
  class MyRMSNorm(RMSNorm): ...
  ```

## Claims

```bash
pytest -v tests/models/transformers/test_layer_registry.py   # 11 passed (1x A100)
```

The new tests cover:
- a plugin override reaching the class the backend builds, with the variable at `0` and `1`, including `GeluAndMul`, which has no hw-agnostic port;
- a missing hw-agnostic module falling back to in-tree, while a broken one raises;
- the in-tree-override warning and the wrong-base `TypeError`.

## Details

- **Opt-in, not rebinding.** Two alternative approaches where tried: A rebinding approach via https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57715 and a re-exporting via https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53153. However, this approach currently seems to be the best trade-off between isolation and user/developer-experience.
- **Fallback is allowed and logged once.** On the hw-agnostic path, a layer with no hw-agnostic port resolves to the in-tree class, with a single warning. The backend falls back the same way, so the override still applies. That lets a plugin switch all its imports to `resolve` at once. A strict mode could be added later as a backward-compatible flag.
- **Only reachable through `vllm.model_executor.hw_agnostic`.** It lives in `hw_agnostic/_resolve.py`. The module name is private so the `resolve` function doesn't shadow the submodule.
- **The check is in the hw-agnostic `__new__`.** A helper shared by `CustomOp` and `PluggableLayer` replaces their duplicated override lookup. The in-tree `CustomOp` is unchanged.
- **Limitations:**
  - `VLLM_USE_HW_AGNOSTIC` only affects the Transformers backend. Models with a native vLLM implementation build the in-tree class even when it is set, so a plugin that also serves them registers its override for the in-tree class too. This is documented in `custom_op.md`.
  - Type checkers reject a variable as a base class. The docs show a `TYPE_CHECKING` pattern for plugins that run mypy.
  - The in-tree `get_act_and_mul_fn` caches the instance it builds first. An activation built before plugins load keeps the un-overridden class. This is unchanged by this PR and doesn't happen in normal startup.

cc @tdoublep @hmellor

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Kimi-K3][Perf] Cut gfx942 MXFP4-to-int4 requant time under pure TP
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Cut the gfx942 Kimi-K3 MXFP4-to-int4 MoE requant (`--quantization-config '{"moe":{"weight":"int4_per_group_32"}}'`, added in #51274) from ~19 min to 25 s under pure TP8. TP8 server startup drops from 22.5 min to 3.5 min. The converted weights are byte-identical.


## Validation

**End to end:** 8x MI325X (gfx942), ROCm 10.0, Kimi-K3 with the DSpark draft. The checkpoint was in the page cache for all startup numbers. Before and after use the same base; only `mxfp4.py` differs.

```bash
VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MLA=1 \
vllm serve moonshotai/Kimi-K3 --trust-remote-code --language-model-only -tp 8 [--enable-expert-parallel] \
  --max-model-len 16384 --max-num-seqs 4 --reasoning-parser kimi_k3 \
  --quantization-config '{"moe":{"weight":"int4_per_group_32"}}' \
  --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE"}' \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"Inferact/Kimi-K3-DSpark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"attention_backend":"TRITON_MLA","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block"}'
```

| Config | Requant before | Requant after | Startup to `/health` before | Startup to `/health` after | KV cache before | KV cache after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP8 | 19 min 15 s | 25 s | 1348 s | 210 s | 27.37 GiB | 28.21 GiB |
| EP8 | 4 min 38 s | 24 s | 431 s | 181 s | 22.57 GiB | 23.41 GiB |

The requant is the time between `Loading weights took` and `Online quantization as part of model loading` on rank 0.

**Accuracy** (GSM8K, 5-shot, `lm_eval --model local-completions`, with the fix):
- TP8: 0.988 ± 0.007 on 250 questions.
- EP8: 1.000 on 100 questions.

The weights are byte-identical to the current code (see below), so I didn't rerun accuracy on the baseline.

**Per-layer microbenchmark:** one full Kimi-K3 MoE layer (w13 + w2), per-rank shapes with `routed_expert_hidden_size` 3584, run under `max_split_size_mb:20` like `gpu_worker.load_model`. Times are the median of 7 runs, alternating before and after. The old code's first run in a fresh process is faster (1.94 s TP8, 0.85 s EP8); its `hipFree` cost grows as the process maps more memory.

| Shape | Time before | Time after | Peak allocated before | after | Peak reserved before | after | `empty_cache()` calls before | after | Byte-identical |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TP8 (896 experts, w13 768 x 3584) | 3.79 s | 0.13 s | 1.56 GiB | 2.89 GiB | 1.85 GiB | 4.56 GiB | 228 | 4 | yes |
| EP8 (112 experts, w13 6144 x 3584) | 3.07 s | 0.30 s | 3.43 GiB | 2.89 GiB | 5.66 GiB | 4.56 GiB | 32 | 4 | yes |

**New test:** `tests/kernels/quantization/test_k3_gfx942_int4_requant.py`. It runs on gfx942 only and is picked up by the existing "(MI300) Quantization Kernels" step. It checks that the output does not depend on chunking, and that no device memory is allocated after the first chunk on the Kimi-K3 TP8 w2 shape under `load_model`'s allocator settings. It passes 4/4 with the fix and fails before it. Against the refactor-only parent (9acd4b58ba), every chunk allocates:

```
E       assert [1724, 1737, ...76, 1789, ...] == [1724, 1724, ...24, 1724, ...]
1 failed, 3 passed
```

Against the first revision of this PR (3bdfe8097f), the shorter last chunk allocates:

```
E       assert [90, 90, 90, 90, 111] == [90, 90, 90, 90, 90]
1 failed, 3 passed
```

For those runs the test loaded `mxfp4.py` from each commit. On the parent I appended `_K3_INT4_CONVERT_CHUNK_VALUES` only so the test's `monkeypatch.setattr` resolves; the old code ignores it.

`tests/models/kimi_k3/test_gfx942_int4.py` and `tests/quantization/test_quantization_config_args.py` still pass.

## Details

**Root cause.** `_setup_kernel_k3_situ_gfx942` converted 8 experts per chunk and called `torch.accelerator.empty_cache()` after every chunk. Pure TP keeps all 896 experts per rank at 1/tp width, so TP8 ran 112 chunks per weight where EP8 runs 14, for the same bytes. That is 20,608 chunks over 92 MoE layers.

Every `empty_cache()` hands the chunk's temporaries back to the driver, and the next chunk allocates them again. In a live TP8 server, a native py-spy profile of the requant showed 92% of the time in `emptyCache -> release_block -> hipFree` (HSA `munmap`/`ioctl`) and about 5% in `hipMalloc`. The conversion kernels themselves barely appeared. That worked out to about 56 ms per chunk.

**Fix.**
- Size each chunk by unpacked values instead of experts, using `_K3_INT4_CONVERT_CHUNK_VALUES = 1 << 27`. TP8 and EP8 both run 19 chunks per w13 and 10 per w2.
- Drop the per-chunk `empty_cache()`, so later chunks reuse the cached temporaries. The cache is still emptied once per converted weight.
- Keep every chunk the same shape by shifting the last chunk back to overlap the previous one. Under `max_split_size_mb:20`, a cached block of 20 MiB or more is only reused for a request less than 20 MiB smaller, so a shorter last chunk would allocate a second set of temporaries. The overlapping experts are recomputed to identical values, which costs less than one chunk per weight.
- The output can't depend on chunk size: `per_1x32_i4_quant`, `shuffle_weight` and `shuffle_scale_for_int4` all work per expert along the leading dimension. The new test checks this explicitly.

**Tradeoffs.** The TP8 per-layer peak grows (allocated 1.56 to 2.89 GiB, reserved 1.85 to 4.56 GiB), because the old TP chunks were tiny. The EP8 peak shrinks (allocated 3.43 to 2.89 GiB, reserved 5.66 to 4.56 GiB). Both stay below the old EP8 peak, which already fit.

commits.pr_title: [Rust Frontend] Support return_prompt_text
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Support `return_prompt_text` on chat completions in the Rust frontend (vllm-project/vllm#42052): the response carries `prompt_text`, the prompt string the chat template produced, on non-streaming responses and on the first stream chunk. The Rust frontend rejected `return_prompt_text: true` with a 400 placeholder from vllm-project/vllm#62434, whose TODO this resolves.

## Claims

| Request | Python | Rust before | Rust after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `return_prompt_text` unset or `false` | `prompt_text: null` (non-streaming; first chunk) | same | same |
| `true`, a renderer that produces text (HF templates, DeepSeek V3.2) | rendered prompt string | 400 | rendered prompt string |
| `true`, multimodal content | rendered string, placeholders not expanded | 400 | same as Python |
| `true`, a renderer that produces token IDs (Harmony and others) | `null` | 400 | `null` |

- Streaming puts it on the first chunk only; later chunks omit the key, as they already do for `prompt_token_ids`.
- The prompt string is copied only for requests that ask for it.

## Validation

Commands from `.buildkite/scripts/run-rust-frontend-cargo-ci.sh` (`style-clippy` and `test`), run from the repo root on this branch:

```
cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all -- --check   # ok
cargo sort --workspace --check rust                          # ok
cargo deny --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --config rust/deny.toml check bans   # ok
cargo clippy --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings   # ok
cargo nextest run --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features --locked --no-fail-fast
# 2385 tests run: 2385 passed, 13 skipped
```

- `routes::tests::chat_return_prompt_text_reports_the_rendered_prompt`: a streaming and a non-streaming request through the router and a mock engine; each returns the fake renderer's `"user: hello\nassistant:"`, and in the stream it appears on the first chunk only.
- `chat_stream_and_collect_preserve_prompt_and_sample_logprobs` (vllm-chat): the stream and `collect_message` both carry the rendered text when requested; `chat_streams_text_events` pins `None` when it is not.
- `non_stream_chat_image_url_reaches_engine_mm_features` also sets `return_prompt_text` and checks for the rendered text with one unexpanded image placeholder.
- Red-green: without the stream-level fill, the route and chat tests fail; with the text captured after placeholder expansion, the multimodal case fails; with the first chunk dropping the text, the streaming test fails.
- The `validate_request_compat_rejects_return_prompt_text` unit test goes away with the placeholder.

## Details

**Layering.** The value is produced by rendering, which belongs to `vllm-chat`, so `ChatRequestProcessor::prepare_text_request` takes it from the `RenderedPrompt` before `finalize_rendered_prompt` expands media placeholders, and only when `ChatRequest::return_prompt_text` is set. It is request metadata, so it reaches the server on `ChatEventStream` (`prompt_text()` and `take_prompt_text()`, next to `request_id()`), set by `ChatLlm::chat`; the chat events and output processors are unchanged. `collect_message` copies it into `CollectedAssistantMessage`, and the streaming route takes it once for the first chunk. `prepare` now returns a named `PreparedChatRequest` instead of a tuple so it can carry the text; the render route takes only `text_request` from it. `vllm-server` only lowers the DTO flag and fills the existing `prompt_text` response fields.

**Differences from Python.**

- With a renderer that produces token IDs, Python reports a detokenized prompt only as a side effect of `echo=true` without `return_token_ids` (`needs_detokenization`), and not at all on its Harmony path. Rust reports `null`: that is an echo implementation detail, not the `return_prompt_text` contract.
- With `truncate_prompt_tokens` and left truncation, Python may report text already pre-trimmed by its character-length guard (a tokenizer performance bound); Rust reports the full rendered prompt.

Not a duplicate: no open PR implements `return_prompt_text` in the Rust frontend (searched open PRs for `return_prompt_text`). AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to prepare this change; the human submitter reviewed every changed line.

commits.pr_title: [KV Connector] Support heterogeneous TP sharing for hybrid KV cache in Mooncake Store
commits.pr_body:
## Dependency

Depends on #53129.

This is a follow-up PR that extends the heterogeneous TP Store layout
introduced in #53129 to unified hybrid KV caches. Please review the
Hybrid-specific commits after #53129. The dependency changes will
disappear from this PR diff after #53129 merges and this branch is
rebased onto upstream `main`.

Merge order:

1. #53129
2. This PR

## Purpose

This PR extends heterogeneous-TP sharing in `MooncakeStoreConnector` from a
single Full Attention cache group to unified Hybrid KV cache allocations. vLLM
instances whose local TP sizes divide a common Store TP size can share the same
Attention KV and Mamba/GDN state through Mooncake Store. Sharing endpoints use
the same PP size.

Hybrid KV cache adds three challenges beyond Full Attention:

- Attention KV grows by token, while Mamba/GDN groups store complete recurrent
  checkpoints with different TP replication rules;
- vLLM aligns Attention pages with Mamba/GDN state pages, so the local page size
  can change with TP size even when two endpoints use the same model;
- prefix reuse must intersect the available boundaries of every cache group,
  while Decode writeback may advance each group at a different rate.

This PR builds on the common Store TP layout from #53129 and represents each
cache group in a stable Store namespace. Attention uses TP-independent Store
chunks, while Mamba/GDN uses complete state checkpoints. These Store boundaries
are independent of the endpoint's local Hybrid page allocation.

### Unified Hybrid Store layout

Each cache group creates its Store layout from its `KVCacheSpec`:

- Attention groups divide global KV head slots into the fixed Store TP shards;
- MQA and replicated GQA use their physical head-slot count for Store sharding;
- Mamba/GDN groups store complete convolution and recurrent state units and
  map replicated local units to their Store shards;
- `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` is unwrapped before the group layout is planned;
- each group namespace includes its Store value format and schema fingerprint.

`StoreLayout` owns tensor interpretation, shard mapping, buffer spans, and Store
keys. The worker executes the resulting descriptors through a common path.

### Attention layouts

The heterogeneous Store path supports the backend-native LBHNC, BLHNC, LHBNC,
BHLNC, LBNHC, and BLNHC cache layouts.

- LBHNC, BLHNC, LHBNC, and BHLNC are normalized to the same head-major Store
  value order;
- LBNHC and BLNHC are normalized to the same token-major Store value order;
- endpoints whose local layouts produce the same Store value order share one
  namespace;
- head-major and token-major Store values remain isolated by their schema.

### Store chunks and local Hybrid pages

`store_chunk_size` defines the stable number of tokens represented by one
Attention Store object. A local Attention page can contain multiple Store
chunks. The connector reads and writes those chunks through tensor-offset
descriptors, so endpoints can share Store objects when their local Hybrid page
sizes differ.

Hybrid heterogeneous-TP sharing requires the same explicit
`--prefix-match-unit` on every endpoint. The connector uses that prefix-hash
boundary as `store_chunk_size` when no Store-specific value is configured. An
explicit larger `store_chunk_size` may reduce Store object and metadata
overhead:

```json
{
    "kv_connector_extra_config": {
        "store_tp_size": 4,
        "store_chunk_size": 400,
        "save_decode_cache": true
    }
}
```

The configured value must be a multiple of `prefix_match_unit`, align with
every stored state, and divide the local Attention page. Invalid or
incompatible configurations use the isolated rank-local Store namespace.

### Hybrid lookup and Decode writeback

Hybrid prefix lookup intersects the availability of all required cache groups
at each reusable boundary. Attention chunks may be stored before the next full
Hybrid checkpoint. Mamba/GDN entries remain complete state snapshots at their
reusable boundaries, so lookup exposes a longer prefix only after every group
required at that boundary is present.

Decode offloading tracks acknowledged progress per cache group. Attention can
advance independently while a Mamba/GDN group waits for its next complete
checkpoint. A failed PUT retries from the earliest unacknowledged offset for
that group. Partial physical cache blocks are stored from their copy-on-write
handoff sources, allowing a hash-aligned Store chunk to be written before its
larger local page is complete.

Scheduler Store-job boundaries, prefix-hash boundaries, local cache pages, and
KV-event block boundaries are resolved independently. KV events continue to
describe the scheduler's logical block chain while Store jobs operate on the
finer Hybrid checkpoint when required.

### Supported scope

Shared endpoints satisfy the compatibility requirements from #53129 and the
following Hybrid constraints:

- Store TP size is greater than or equal to local TP size and divisible by it;
- all sharing endpoints use the same Store TP size and PP size;
- Attention head slots and Store shards have an integral divisible mapping;
- cache groups use supported Attention specs or `MambaSpec`, including
  supported `UniformTypeKVCacheSpecs` wrappers;
- Mamba/GDN convolution state uses DS or SD layout; sharing endpoints use the
  same layout;
- PCP and DCP are disabled;
- cross-layer KV blocks are disabled.

Endpoints outside this scope retain the existing rank-local behavior.

This PR updates the Mooncake Store Connector documentation and adds regression
coverage for:

- mixed Attention and Mamba/GDN cache groups;
- per-group TP replication and Store-shard ownership;
- all six backend-native Attention cache layouts;
- head-major and token-major Store schema normalization;
- TP-independent Store chunk selection and explicit `store_chunk_size`;
- Hybrid local pages containing multiple Store chunks;
- partial-tail PUT and GET from copy-on-write cache blocks;
- per-group acknowledged Store progress and PUT retries;
- prefix lookup across cache groups with different reusable boundaries;
- scheduler Store-job, prefix-hash, and KV-event boundary separation;
- rank-local fallback for unsupported or incompatible configurations.

## Related Issues and PRs

- Issue #45036 tracks the Mooncake Store Connector roadmap, including Decode
  KV PUT and heterogeneous GQA/TP sharing. This PR extends that work to Hybrid
  KV cache allocations with divisible TP sizes.
- PR #52466 added Decode KV offloading to Mooncake Store consumers. This PR
  applies the same consumer writeback lifecycle independently across Hybrid
  cache groups.
- PR #53129 introduces the common Store TP layout for Full Attention KV cache.
  This PR uses that layout as its base and extends the Store planning,
  namespace, lookup, and writeback paths to Hybrid KV cache.
- PR #53078 adds heterogeneous-TP support for Hybrid GDN/Mamba models to
  `MooncakeConnector` direct P/D transfer. This PR targets persistent and
  reusable KV objects in `MooncakeStoreConnector`, including prefix lookup and
  Decode writeback through a shared Store pool.

## Test Plan

### Unit and static checks

```bash
pre-commit run --files \
  docs/features/mooncake_store_connector_usage.md \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_layout.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_worker.py \
  vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/store/data.py \
  vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/store/scheduler.py \
  vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/mooncake/store/worker.py \
  vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/ssm_conv_transfer_utils.py

python -m pytest -q \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_layout.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_worker.py \
  tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_mooncake_store_hma_e2e.py
```

### RDMA cluster tests

Reusable E2E test code:

- [Hybrid heterogeneous-TP cluster tests](https://github.com/ScaleX-IO/vllm/tree/decode-offloading-e2e-tests/examples/disaggregated/mooncake_store_connector/hybrid_heterogeneous_tp_cluster)
- [Falcon-H1 Hybrid boundary tests](https://github.com/ScaleX-IO/vllm/tree/5575f4bc9093c7a423e5914e709c3cbaf2029b01/examples/disaggregated/mooncake_store_connector/falcon_h1_hybrid_heterogeneous_tp_cluster)

Environment:

- Alibaba Cloud Linux 3, x86_64;
- Python 3.12.13;
- PyTorch 2.13.0 with CUDA 13.0;
- NVIDIA driver 580.105.08;
- one compute node with NVIDIA H20 GPUs and NVLink;
- RDMA transport through `mlx5_bond_0`;
- standalone Mooncake Store with RDMA transport;
- eager vLLM execution with prefix caching enabled;
- fixed `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` across Store endpoints.

The main checkpoint matrix uses Falcon-H1-0.5B-Instruct, whose cache contains
Attention KV together with Mamba convolution and recurrent state. TP1 and TP2
both resolve an 800-token local Hybrid page. Store TP is 2 and the default
Store chunk is the explicitly configured 16-token prefix match unit.

Every case uses a connector-free reference at the consumer TP size. The test
checks cached-token boundaries, compares the first 64 generated token IDs with
the same-TP reference, waits for asynchronous Store jobs, and verifies Decode
writeback with a fresh Store lookup.

## Test Result

### Unit and static checks

```text
All selected pre-commit hooks passed.
35 focused Mooncake Store Hybrid/layout tests passed.
11 existing NIXL Mamba conv-split tests passed.
```

### RDMA cluster tests

Falcon-H1 Hybrid boundary results:

| Producer -> consumer | Prompt tokens | Initial Store hit | Decode tokens | Fresh extended hit | Reference tokens | Failed keys |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: |
| TP2 -> TP1 | 801 | 800 | 816 | 1,600 | First 64 match | 0 |
| TP1 -> TP2 | 801 | 800 | 816 | 1,600 | First 64 match | 0 |
| TP2 -> TP1, short Decode | 801 | 800 | 64 | 800 | All 64 match | 0 |
| TP2 -> TP1, Store boundary | 799 | 784 | 64 | 800 | All 64 match | 0 |

The long Decode cases cross the next complete Hybrid checkpoint and verify
writeback in both TP directions. The short case confirms that early Attention
PUT does not expose an incomplete Mamba checkpoint. The 799-token case verifies
the 16-token Store boundary independently from the 800-token local Hybrid page.

An additional explicit `store_chunk_size=400` matrix passed in both TP4 -> TP2
and TP2 -> TP4 directions. Each 1,601-token prompt hit 1,600 tokens, Decode
generated 816 tokens, and the fresh reverse lookup hit 2,400 tokens. The first
64 output token IDs matched the same-TP references, and Mooncake reported zero
failed keys or operation errors.

Qwen3.5 Hybrid results:

| Producer -> consumer | Prompt tokens | Initial Store hit | Decode tokens | Fresh extended hit | Reference tokens | Failed keys |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: |
| TP4 -> TP2 | 785 | 784 | 800 | 1,568 | First 64 match | 0 |
| TP2 -> TP4 | 785 | 784 | 800 | 1,568 | First 64 match | 0 |

Both directions reused the Store prefix, crossed the next complete Hybrid
checkpoint, and loaded Decode-written state through a fresh lookup. Mooncake
reported zero failed keys and operation errors.

---

commits.pr_title: [Rust Frontend] Report completion_tokens_details only when reasoning tokens are counted
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Report `usage.completion_tokens_details` only when the Rust frontend can count reasoning tokens, as the Python frontend does: on chat with a reasoning parser. Elsewhere it is now `null` instead of `{"reasoning_tokens": 0}`.

## Claims

| Route | Before | After (Python) |
|---|---|---|
| chat, reasoning parser configured | `{"reasoning_tokens": N}` | unchanged |
| chat, no reasoning parser | `{"reasoning_tokens": 0}` | `null` |
| completions, generate | `{"reasoning_tokens": 0}` | `null` |

## Validation

Commands from `.buildkite/scripts/run-rust-frontend-cargo-ci.sh` (`style-clippy` and `test`), run from the repo root on this branch:

```
cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all -- --check   # ok
cargo sort --workspace --check rust                          # ok
cargo deny --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --config rust/deny.toml check bans   # ok
cargo clippy --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings   # ok
cargo nextest run --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features --locked --no-fail-fast
# 2374 tests run: 2374 passed, 13 skipped
```

New or changed tests:

- `usage_tests::token_usage_serializes_reasoning_token_details_only_when_counted`: `Some(3)`, `Some(0)` and `None` serialize as Python does.
- `chunk_stream_reports_reasoning_token_details_only_with_reasoning_parser`: every streamed usage reports `{"reasoning_tokens": 0}` with a reasoning parser and `null` without one.
- `non_stream_chat_returns_json_response` and `non_stream_completions_return_json_response` (HTTP, mock engine): `usage.completion_tokens_details` is an explicit `null`.
- `include_reasoning_false_suppresses_reasoning_in_non_stream_chat` (HTTP, auto-selected `qwen3` reasoning parser): hidden reasoning is still counted, `{"reasoning_tokens": 5}`.

Restoring the zero-filled details fails the first four tests; forcing the route's reasoning count off fails the last one.

E2E: `tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_chat.py::test_single_chat_session` and `tests/entrypoints/serve/instrumentator/test_orca_metrics.py::test_single_completion` compare the whole usage with `CompletionUsage(...)` without details, and fail under the Rust frontend on `main` because of the zero-filled details.

## Details

Python sets `_include_reasoning_tokens_details = bool(reasoning_parser)` in `OpenAIServingChat` (vllm-project/vllm#45802); completions and generate never build the details. Rust always reported `{"reasoning_tokens": 0}`, because completions and generate share the chat `Usage` type, and vllm-project/vllm#54883 made the details always serialized. That claims zero reasoning where the frontend cannot count any: `null` means unknown.

- `Usage.completion_tokens_details` is `Option<CompletionTokenUsageInfo>`; `Usage::from_token_usage` takes the engine `TokenUsage` and the reasoning count as `Option<usize>`. It still destructures `TokenUsage` and `PromptCacheUsage` exhaustively, as in vllm-project/vllm#63292.
- The chat route counts reasoning tokens when `ChatLlm::reasoning_parser_name()` is set (the effective parser after `auto` resolution) and passes that to response collection and streaming. `ContinuousUsage` carries the count only when counting. Completions and generate pass `None`.

**Layering.** The usage shape is built in the `vllm-server` response layer, where Python's serving class makes the same decision from its configured reasoning parser; the reasoning count itself still comes from `vllm-chat`.

**Deviation.** Python dumps usage-only stream chunks with `exclude_none=True`, so it omits the key there, while Rust serializes `null`, as it already does for `prompt_tokens_details` on stream chunks; omitting unset stream keys is a separate follow-up.

Not a duplicate: overlaps vllm-project/vllm#63780, a first-time contributor's PR that changes chat stream key presence, including these details on chat streams. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to prepare this change; the human submitter reviewed every changed line.

- With the variable set (`1` or `true`, case-insensitive, trimmed, as Python parses it), an unknown `model` is accepted and served by the base model on chat, completions, `/inference/v1/generate`, `/tokenize`, `/detokenize`, gRPC and the render server, and the response's `model` is the primary served name, as in Python.

- `lora::tests::resolve_model_selects_adapter_when_any_model_name_is_accepted`: with skip on, an adapter name still selects the adapter, and an unknown name selects none but is accepted.
- `routes::tests::skip_model_name_validation_serves_unknown_model_with_base_model`: chat with `"model": "wrong-model"` returns 200 with `model` set to the primary name; `/tokenize` accepts it.
- The CLI env-only-settings tests for `serve`, `--args-json` and `render` cover the default, `1`/`TRUE`, and a non-truthy value.

## Details

Python reads the variable in `OpenAIServing._is_model_supported` (`vllm/entrypoints/serve/engine/serving.py`), which every `_check_model` caller goes through.

- **One owner for the decision.** A new `ServedModelNames` (`server/src/model_names.rs`) holds the selectable names (served base names, then loaded LoRA adapters; primary first) and whether any other name is accepted. Its `accepts`/`check` replace five hand-written membership checks in the chat, completions and generate validators, `/tokenize` and `/detokenize`, and gRPC `to_text_request`. `LoraManager::resolve_model` extends the base names with the adapters, so LoRA selection is unchanged and still wins over the skip.

**Layering.** The accepted-name set is a property of the server (base names fixed at startup, adapters from the LoRA registry), so the type lives in `vllm-server` next to the LoRA registry, and each protocol entry point only asks it. The env var is read where the other frontend-read env vars are read, in `vllm-cmd`.

**Merge note.** vllm-project/vllm#64513 (generate response envelope) extracts the same response-model expression in chat and completions `convert.rs`; whichever lands second is a one-line rebase.

commits.pr_title: [Rust Frontend] Log one structured access log event per HTTP response
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Log one structured INFO event per HTTP response on the Rust frontend, and make `--disable-uvicorn-access-log` and `--disable-access-log-for-endpoints` real options instead of no-ops. Python's API server logs one uvicorn access line per response by default; the Rust frontend logged none, so a deployment moved to it lost its request log.

## Claims

- Every response gets one INFO event once its head is ready, including 401s from API-key auth and 404s for unknown routes; a streaming response is logged once, when its stream starts:

  ```text
  HTTP response client=127.0.0.1:52344 method=GET uri="/v1/models?limit=1" version=HTTP/1.1 status=200 latency=1.2ms
  ```

  `client` is absent on a Unix-domain socket, and `latency` covers the time until the response head is ready, not a streamed body.
- `--disable-access-log` (with `--disable-uvicorn-access-log` as a visible alias) turns it off, on `vllm-rs serve` and on the Python launcher path.
- `--disable-access-log-for-endpoints /health,/metrics` drops responses whose path, without the query string, matches exactly; the list is split on commas and trimmed like Python's.

## Validation

Commands from `.buildkite/scripts/run-rust-frontend-cargo-ci.sh` (`style-clippy` and `test`), run from the repo root on this branch:

```
cargo fmt --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --all -- --check   # ok
cargo sort --workspace --check rust                          # ok
cargo deny --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --config rust/deny.toml check bans   # ok
cargo clippy --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings   # ok
cargo nextest run --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features --locked --no-fail-fast
# 2381 tests run: 2381 passed, 13 skipped
```

- `routes::tests::access_log_records_each_response`: through `build_router` with an API key and `/version` excluded, it sends a 200 with a client address and a query string, an unauthenticated 401, an unrouted 404, and an excluded `/version?verbose=1`, and snapshots exactly three events with their fields (latency shown only as present). It fails when the layer is not installed, and also when the exclusion is skipped.
- `routes::tests::access_log_disabled_logs_nothing`: no event with the access log disabled.
- `cli::tests::frontend_args_json_passes_access_log_flags_into_config`: the defaults, and both flags from `--args-json` with Python's key and a comma-separated list (`"/health, /metrics,"`).
- `cli::tests::serve_disable_access_log_accepts_python_flag_name`: on `vllm-rs serve`, `--disable-access-log` and `--disable-uvicorn-access-log` both disable it, and `--disable-access-log=false` keeps it.
- `tls_tests::plain_http_exposes_tcp_peer_as_connect_info`: over a real TCP connection through `serve_connections`, a handler sees the peer as `ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>`.
- Six CLI snapshots of parsed args and configs gain the new fields (refreshed with `UPDATE_EXPECT=1`; the diff adds only those fields).

## Details

Python logs through uvicorn's access logger at INFO, on by default. `--disable-uvicorn-access-log` turns it off, and `--disable-access-log-for-endpoints` drops responses by exact path match (`UvicornAccessLogFilter` in `vllm/logging_utils/uvicorn_logging.py`, built by `get_uvicorn_log_config` in `vllm/entrypoints/launchers/utils/server_utils.py`). uvicorn logs when the response head is sent, so every response gets a line. The Rust frontend declared both flags as no-ops, and its `TraceLayer` logs requests only at DEBUG.

- New `middleware::log_access` emits the event, layered outside auth next to `TraceLayer`, so rejected and unrouted requests are logged as uvicorn logs them.
- Both flags are real options on `SharedRuntimeArgs`. They reach Rust through `--args-json` under the Python launcher (a serde alias accepts Python's `disable_uvicorn_access_log` key) and are parsed into a new `AccessLogConfig` on `Config` and `AppState`, which follows the `CorsConfig` path.
- The hand-rolled serve loop now inserts the TCP peer into each request as axum's `ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>`, as `axum::serve` does, so the event carries the client address.

**Layering.** The access log describes HTTP exchanges, so it lives in the server's middleware stack, the only layer that sees every response including those auth or routing reject. The peer address is known only in the serve loop, which exposes it through the standard axum extension rather than a new type.

**Why not raise `TraceLayer` to INFO.** Its default span and `on_response` event already carry method, URI, version, status and latency. But the vLLM log formatter prints every enabled span in scope as a prefix, so an INFO span would prefix every request-scoped log line (output logs, warnings, the chat `request_id` span) with the HTTP fields, and the access log flag would change the shape of unrelated log lines. `TraceLayer` stays at DEBUG.

**Flag names.** There is no uvicorn in the Rust frontend, so the canonical flag is `--disable-access-log`. The Python name stays as a visible alias: `vllm-rs serve` routes only long names and visible aliases to the frontend (`collect_option_names` in `vllm-managed-engine`) and passes anything else through to Python, so a hidden alias would silently do nothing. Python's `--no-disable-uvicorn-access-log` form is not accepted, like the `no-` forms of the other real bool flags; the launcher never forwards it, since it sends only non-default values.

**Differences from Python.**

- The access log is a structured `tracing` event, not uvicorn's request line; the same facts (client, method, target, version, status) are fields, plus `latency`, and the status has no reason phrase.
- IPv6 clients print as `[::1]:52344` (Rust's `SocketAddr`), where uvicorn prints `::1:52344`.
- The path is printed raw as received, where uvicorn re-quotes the decoded path; the two are the same for ordinary ASCII paths.
- `--uvicorn-log-level` stays unsupported. In Python it also sets the access logger's level; in Rust, `RUST_LOG=vllm_server::middleware::access_log=warn` silences the access log on its own.
- Not covered: routes merged through `serve_with_router_extension` sit outside every layer `build_router` installs (auth, HTTP metrics, CORS, `TraceLayer`), and the engine-free `vllm-rs render` server has its own narrow flag set and serve loop. Both are separate follow-ups.

Behavior change: existing Rust-frontend deployments now get one INFO event per response by default, as Python deployments get one line.

Not a duplicate: supersedes the inactive vllm-project/vllm#48138 (no activity since 2026-08-06). Like that draft, it adds a middleware and makes both flags real; unlike it, the event carries the client address and latency as structured fields. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used to prepare this change; the human submitter reviewed every changed line.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][SleepMode] Exact-size, reusable pinned CPU backup for level-1 sleep
commits.pr_body:
## Problem

Level-1 sleep backs up every cumem allocation to host memory with `torch.empty(size, pin_memory=True)`. torch's `CachingHostAllocator` rounds each pinned block up to a power of two and keeps freed blocks in its cache, so the level-1 backup costs up to ~2x the offloaded bytes in host memory, and that memory is never returned to the OS. On Mistral Large 4 at TP8 the backup is 85.19 GiB per GPU, which turned into roughly +578 GiB of host memory per node.

## Root cause

The backup size is chosen by the caching host allocator, not by the allocation. The old code already kept the memory across wake-ups: the freed pinned block stayed in the cache and was handed back on the next sleep, which is why repeated sleeps were fast. The bug is the rounding. Nothing in this path asks for the cache.

## Fix

Data model: `AllocationData.cpu_backup_tensor` is the allocation's host backup buffer, one per allocation.

- Lifetime: created exact-size on the first level-1 offload of that allocation, reused on every later offload, released only when the allocation is freed or its contents are discarded (level-2 sleep, tags not offloaded, `discard()`).
- Validity is derived, not stored: wake restores an allocation iff it is asleep and has a buffer.
- Invariant: asleep + buffer => the buffer holds this sleep's data. Every transition to asleep (`sleep` and `discard`) goes through one helper, `_put_to_sleep(ptr, data, offload)`, which either copies into the buffer or releases it before unmapping. So a buffer left over from an earlier offload can never be restored after a discard. The existing already-asleep policy checks (`cpu_backup_tensor is not None` on asleep allocations) keep their meaning unchanged.
- CUDA/ROCm (`cumem.py`): the buffer is an anonymous `mmap` wrapped with `torch.frombuffer` and pinned with the existing `libcudart.cudaHostRegister` wrapper. If registration fails, the error is drained with `cudaGetLastError`, a warning is logged once and the backup stays pageable, the same fallback as the other `cudaHostRegister` callers (`shm_tensor_arena.py`, `ec_shared_region.py`). Release unregisters only a pinned buffer, ignores the return code (draining any error) and never raises, since it also runs from the allocator's free callback; then the reference is dropped, which unmaps it.
- XPU (`xpumem.py`): same single-field reuse/release semantics with its existing pinned torch tensor. Exact-size pinning is not available there.

No config, env var, API or protocol change. None is needed: the old behavior already kept the backup memory between sleeps, and this keeps it at exactly the offloaded size.

## Results

Qwen3-8B, 1x GB200, `enable_sleep_mode=True`, 4 cycles of `sleep(level=1)`, `wake_up()` and greedy generate. Host memory is node `MemTotal - MemAvailable` relative to before the first sleep.

| | host asleep | host awake | first sleep | later sleeps | wake | outputs identical |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main | 23.00 GiB | 22.99 GiB | 1.16 s | 0.16-0.18 s | 0.13-0.14 s | yes (4/4) |
| this PR | 16.92 GiB | 16.92 GiB | 0.84 s | 0.15 s | 0.13 s | yes (4/4) |

Host memory is flat across cycles in both cases. Sleep and wake are as fast as before.

## Test plan

No new test function; the existing tests in `tests/basic_correctness/memory/cumem/test_cumem.py` are strengthened with deterministic checks (no RSS thresholds). Every level-1 backup must be exactly its allocation's size and page-locked, and torch's pinned host caching allocator must not be used across sleep (`torch.cuda.host_memory_stats()["allocated_bytes.allocated"]` unchanged).

- `test_release_kv_cache_memory_preserves_generation` (kv-only / sleep-1 / sleep-2) and `test_sleep_with_only_weights_asleep` (first x second level): 3 and 2 sleep/wake cycles with greedy output identical to pre-sleep every cycle. Worker-side state is read via `collective_rpc`: offloaded tags hold exact pinned backups and others hold none; the same buffers are kept after wake and reused on the next sleep; a level-1 then level-2 cycle leaves weights with no backup.
- `test_basic_cumem` (`pinned` / `register-fails`): 3 level-1 cycles with changing data, same buffers reused. A sleep that does not offload the tag releases (unregisters) its backup. Freeing an allocation releases its backup. In `register-fails`, `cudaHostRegister` returns an error: sleep/wake data is still correct, backups are pageable, a warning is logged, and release never calls `cudaHostUnregister`.
- `test_discard_tags`: `discard()` releases the kv backup, so the following wake has nothing stale to restore; weights keep and reuse theirs.
- `test_level2_discards_ordinary_tensor_with_weights_tag`: level-1 cycle, then a level-2 style sleep releases the backup; the poisoned wake proves nothing was restored.
- `test_reentered_tag`: freeing an offloaded allocation while awake releases its backup.
- `test_runtime_state_survives_sleep`: runtime backups are exact, pinned and kept at both levels without the host caching allocator.

## Test result (GB200)

- With this PR: full `test_cumem.py` 22 passed, 3 runs in a row; `test_basic_cumem[pinned]` and `test_basic_cumem[register-fails]` also pass run alone. `register-fails` fails on the previous revision of this PR, which raised on a registration failure.
- Same tests against main's `cumem.py`: 13 failed, 8 passed. Failing: `test_basic_cumem`, `test_release_kv_cache_memory_preserves_generation[sleep-1,sleep-2]`, `test_sleep_with_only_weights_asleep[all 4]`, `test_runtime_state_survives_sleep[sleep-1,sleep-2]` (torch host caching allocator used during sleep: +32 MiB to +2.5 GB), and `test_discard_tags`, `test_reentered_tag[both]`, `test_level2_discards_ordinary_tensor_with_weights_tag` (backups dropped on wake). With the host-stats check neutralized, the same 13 still fail on backup reuse.
- Engine smoke: see the table above.

XPU change is untested on hardware.

Follow-up option: an opt-in "release the backup on wake" for host-memory-constrained colocated RL is one extra `release_cpu_backup` after the restore copy in `wake_up`. The invariant still holds because it only constrains asleep allocations. Not part of this PR.
